article:
# How to Taste Good When Kissing (Clean Beats Sweet) You showered. You brushed. There's a mint in your pocket and you've checked it twice. Then dinner happens: the garlic bread, the second glass of red, the espresso nobody really needed. By the time the moment arrives, you have no idea what your mouth is serving. Here's what nobody tells you: learning how to taste good when kissing has very little to do with tasting *like* anything. The best kiss barely tastes of anything at all. It's clean, it's comfortably wet, and nothing in it competes with the person. This guide covers what a kiss actually tastes like, why the last thing you ate matters more than the toothpaste you used at six o'clock, what coffee and wine do to your mouth, and the one-minute fixes that work. It also covers the awkward version: what to do when they're the one who tastes off. ## How to Taste Good When Kissing: The Short Answer Aim for neutral, not sweet. Here's the whole plan in five steps:
  1. Brush your teeth and your tongue before you head out. Not in the five minutes before dinner, and not in the five minutes before the kiss. Give the toothpaste time to fade.
  2. Follow the Two-Sip Rule. Every coffee, cocktail or glass of wine gets two sips of plain water after it.
  3. Follow the Last Bite Rule. End the meal on something crisp and raw, like apple or a few mint leaves, rather than on the garlic.
  4. Chew sugar-free gum after you eat, then bin it. Gum belongs after dinner, never during the kiss.
  5. Keep your lips in a light, low-scent balm. Skip the sticky gloss and the tingly medicated stick.
That's the whole system. Everything below explains why each step works, and what to do when real life (a steakhouse, a long flight, a third espresso) gets in the way. ## What a Kiss Actually Tastes Like A kiss tastes like the inside of someone's mouth at that exact moment. Their saliva, whatever they last ate or drank, and their breath, which your nose picks up before your tongue does. And people notice. When psychologists Susan Hughes, Marissa Harrison and Gordon Gallup [surveyed college students about kissing](https://doi.org/10.1177/147470490700500310) for a 2007 paper, they asked how important the taste of someone's mouth is when deciding whether to keep kissing them, on a scale from 0 (not at all) to 4 (extremely). Women averaged 3.00, which on that scale means "very important." Men averaged 2.67. Breath scored higher still: 3.09 for women and 2.88 for men when deciding whether to kiss or keep kissing someone. The authors' own theory is that kissing brings two people close enough to smell and taste each other, which is one of the ways we size up a partner. You don't need to buy the evolutionary story to take the practical point. Taste and breath get judged, and they get judged early. There's also a lot going on in there. A [2014 study in the journal Microbiome](https://doi.org/10.1186/2049-2618-2-41) followed 21 couples and estimated that a single 10-second intimate kiss transfers around 80 million bacteria. That's no reason to panic. It's a reminder that a mouth is a living environment, not a flavor you apply. You can't make it taste like strawberries. You can keep it clean, wet and quiet. If that side of things fascinates you, [the science of kissing](/blog/science-of-kissing/) goes much further into why we do this at all. ## Why Taste Is Mostly Smell Let me be direct. Most of what your partner "tastes" is actually smell. The [National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders](https://www.nidcd.nih.gov/health/taste-disorders) explains that chewing releases aromas that travel up to the nose, which is why food tastes bland when a cold blocks your nose. It also notes that many people who think they've lost their sense of taste have actually lost their sense of smell. During a kiss, your faces are inches apart and you're both breathing. Their nose is right there. That's why a kiss can taste "off" even when your teeth are spotless: the problem is usually something your mouth is giving off, not something sitting on your tongue. Three things cause almost all of it: - **Residue:** food and drink still in your mouth, or in the case of garlic and onion, already in your bloodstream. - **Dryness:** a dry mouth stops rinsing itself, so odor builds. - **Coating:** bacteria living on the back of your tongue. Fix those three and you've done most of the job. For a full breath routine, see the [fresh breath before kissing guide](/blog/fresh-breath-before-kissing/). And if you tend to hold your breath mid-kiss and then exhale all at once, [how to breathe while kissing](/blog/how-to-breathe-while-kissing/) is worth five minutes. ## The Neutral Mouth Rule: Why Clean Beats Sweet Here's the most common mistake: trying to taste good by tasting *of something*. A mouthful of candy. Cinnamon gum chewed right up to the front door. Toothpaste so fresh it stings. The person kissing you isn't looking for a flavor. They're looking for you. Strong flavors get in the way, and sugary ones leave a sticky film behind. The Neutral Mouth Rule is simple: **the goal is a mouth that tastes like nothing in particular.** Clean, comfortably wet, a faint trace of mint at most. > The best-tasting kiss is the one that doesn't taste like dinner. There's a reason not to brush right before you eat or kiss, too. Most toothpastes contain sodium lauryl sulfate, the foaming agent, and [Scientific American explains](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/why-does-orange-juice-taste-bad-after-you-brush-your-teeth/) that it dulls your ability to taste sweetness and makes things taste more bitter for a while afterward. It's why orange juice tastes awful after brushing. Brush right before dinner and your food tastes worse. Brush right before the kiss and your partner gets a mouthful of foam. Brushing before you leave the house gets you the clean mouth without either problem. Want your kiss to taste a little sweet? Borrow a hint. A lightly flavored lip balm or a mild mint is plenty. Go further than that and you're serving dessert, not a kiss. ## The Last Bite Rule: What to Eat Before Kissing Your partner tastes your most recent meal far more than anything before it. That's the Last Bite Rule: **whatever you eat last is what gets kissed.** Some foods cheat. According to the [Mayo Clinic](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/bad-breath/symptoms-causes/syc-20350922), once garlic and onions are digested, they enter your bloodstream, get carried to your lungs and affect your breath. That's why brushing after garlic bread doesn't fully fix it. The smell isn't only in your mouth anymore. You can still fight back. Food scientists at Ohio State University [tested what helps with garlic breath](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2016/09/160923083806.htm) and found that raw apple and raw lettuce cut the odor compounds by 50 percent or more for the first 30 minutes. Raw mint leaves did best of all. Green tea, despite its reputation, had no effect on most of them. That gives you a practical menu: - **Finish on something crisp and raw.** An apple, a side salad, a dessert built on fresh fruit, a few mint leaves. - **Go easy on garlic and onion near the end.** You don't have to avoid them all night. Just don't make them the last thing. - **Watch the clingy stuff.** Caramel, sticky sauces and anything that lodges between teeth. A quick swish of water afterward helps. - **If you can still taste it, they can.** Run your tongue around your mouth. If dinner is still in there, rinse. That last check matters even more if you have braces or a beard, because food has more places to hide. See [how to kiss with braces](/blog/how-to-kiss-with-braces/) and [how to kiss someone with a beard](/blog/how-to-kiss-someone-with-a-beard/) for the specifics. ## What Your Drink Does to the Kiss Food gets the blame, but the glass in your hand often does more damage. Most classic date drinks dry your mouth, and a dry mouth tastes stale. ### Coffee Coffee hits twice. The flavor lingers, and the [Mayo Clinic](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/dry-mouth/diagnosis-treatment/drc-20356052) advises people with dry mouth to limit caffeine because it can make the mouth drier. A coffee date isn't a kiss-killer. The cup just shouldn't be the last thing you sip. ### Wine, beer and cocktails Mayo lists [alcohol use among the causes of dry mouth](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/dry-mouth/symptoms-causes/syc-20356048), and it advises against alcohol-based mouthwash for the same reason. Red wine also leaves that puckered, dusty feeling on your tongue and can tint your lips. Sugary cocktails leave sugar behind. ### The Two-Sip Rule This is the simplest fix in the whole article. **After every coffee, cocktail or glass of wine, take two sips of plain water.** It rinses away what's left and keeps your mouth from drying out, which matches Mayo's own dry-mouth advice to sip water throughout the day. One caveat: hydrated doesn't mean flooded. You want a mouth that's comfortable, not one that turns the kiss into a puddle. If that's your worry, [too much saliva when kissing](/blog/too-much-saliva-when-kissing/) has you covered. ## Gum and Mints: Use Them, Then Lose Them Gum is genuinely useful. The [American Dental Association](https://www.mouthhealthy.org/all-topics-a-z/chewing-gum) says chewing sugarless gum for 20 minutes after a meal increases saliva flow, and that saliva helps wash away food and debris. That's exactly what you want after dinner. The catch: gum has no place in the kiss itself. Chew it after you eat, then get rid of it well before the moment arrives. Nobody wants to negotiate around a wad of spearmint, and a strong artificial flavor works against the Neutral Mouth Rule. Mints follow the same logic. A mild one beats an extra-strong one. A mouth full of menthol is a shock for the other person and a fairly obvious sign that you were covering something. The smoothest version? Offer one to both of you. "Want a mint? I'm having one" reads as generous, not as a hint. For a rundown of which mints and gums actually help, the [fresh breath guide](/blog/fresh-breath-before-kissing/) covers it. ## Your Lips Are Part of the Taste Your lips are the first thing they taste, so whatever is on them gets noticed first. - **A light, low-scent balm** keeps lips smooth without a strong flavor. - **Medicated balms can wait.** That cooling sting is lovely on chapped lips and odd on someone else's mouth. - **Sticky gloss** tastes like gloss and leaves residue on both of you. Lipstick has its own rules, which [how to kiss with lipstick on](/blog/how-to-kiss-with-lipstick-on/) walks through. For prep, see [how to make your lips soft for kissing](/blog/how-to-make-your-lips-soft-for-kissing/), and for why every texture and taste registers so strongly there, read [why lips are so sensitive](/blog/why-lips-are-so-sensitive/). ## Don't Skip Your Tongue Most people brush their teeth and stop. The [Mayo Clinic](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/bad-breath/symptoms-causes/syc-20350922) notes that your tongue can trap bacteria that produce odors, and its [treatment advice](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/bad-breath/diagnosis-treatment/drc-20350925) is to brush your tongue along with your teeth. Mayo adds that a tongue scraper may help if your tongue is coated from an overgrowth of bacteria, such as from smoking or dry mouth. Brush gently from back to front. It takes less than a minute, and it's the step most people skip. ## A Date-Night Timeline Put it all together and the evening looks like this:
  1. Before you leave: brush your teeth and tongue, floss, and put on a light balm.
  2. At dinner: keep a glass of water going alongside everything else and follow the Two-Sip Rule.
  3. Last course: end on something crisp, like fruit or a salad, rather than the garlic.
  4. After the meal: chew sugar-free gum to get saliva flowing.
  5. Before the moment: gum out, a sip of water, a quick tongue check. If dinner is still there, rinse.
Five steps, none longer than a minute. That's the entire cost of tasting good. ## If You Smoke This one deserves a straight answer. The [Mayo Clinic](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/bad-breath/symptoms-causes/syc-20350922) says smoking causes its own unpleasant mouth odor, and that smokers and oral tobacco users are more likely to have gum disease, another source of bad breath. Mayo also lists tobacco among the things that make dry mouth worse. Mints and gum won't fully cover it, and a partner who doesn't smoke will notice. The considerate options are to skip the cigarette in the hours before you see them, brush and rinse when you can, and talk about it openly rather than hoping they won't mind. ## When They're the One Who Tastes Off Sometimes you're the one getting the garlic. Here's how to handle it without a scene. - **Share, don't hand over.** Offering a mint to both of you turns a fix into a moment instead of a verdict. - **Slow down rather than pull away.** Shorter, closed-mouth kisses buy time. - **Talk later, privately.** If it's a pattern, bring it up kindly and nowhere near the moment. The fresh breath guide has a full section on [what to do when they have bad breath](/blog/fresh-breath-before-kissing/#the-they-have-bad-breath-problem), and [how to tell someone they're a bad kisser](/blog/how-to-tell-someone-theyre-a-bad-kisser/) helps with the wording for harder conversations. For first-thing-in-the-morning kisses, see [kissing with morning breath](/blog/kissing-with-morning-breath/). ## When Brushing Doesn't Fix It If you do everything here and your mouth still tastes bad, it may not be a habit problem. The [Mayo Clinic](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/bad-breath/symptoms-causes/syc-20350922) lists causes that no mint will solve, including dry mouth from certain medicines, gum disease, infections in the mouth, postnasal drip from sinus problems, and acid reflux (GERD). If bad breath sticks around, see your dentist. If they rule out a dental cause, they may refer you to your doctor. That's a health question, not a kissing one, and it's worth answering. ## The Bottom Line How to taste good when kissing comes down to one idea: clean beats sweet. Brush your teeth and tongue before you head out, give every drink two sips of water, end the meal on something crisp, and bin the gum before the moment. None of it takes more than a minute. Curious how the rest of your kiss is doing? One of the ten questions on [the Kiss Test](/kiss-test/) is a housekeeping round on breath and moisture, and "mint in pocket, checked twice" is one of the answers. If that one sounds familiar, you're in good company. And if you want the fundamentals in one place, the 10 Kiss Commandments chapter is free, just below. ## Frequently Asked Questions ### How do I make my mouth taste good for kissing? Brush your teeth and tongue before you go out, drink water alongside anything else you drink, end your meal on something crisp like apple or fresh mint, and spit out any gum before the kiss. The goal is a clean, neutral mouth rather than a sweet or strongly minty one. ### How can I make my kiss taste sweet? A lightly flavored lip balm or a mild mint gives a hint of sweetness without overpowering anything. Avoid candy, sugary cocktails and sticky gloss right before a kiss, because they leave residue behind. A clean mouth with a trace of flavor tastes better than a mouthful of sugar. ### What does kissing taste like? A kiss tastes like the inside of the other person's mouth at that moment: their saliva, whatever they last ate or drank, and their breath. Because so much of flavor is really smell, breath plays a bigger part than most people expect. A clean mouth tastes close to neutral. ### Can someone taste coffee or alcohol when you kiss them? Often, yes. Both linger, and both can dry out your mouth, which makes it taste stale. Two sips of plain water after each coffee or drink rinses away what's left and keeps your mouth comfortable. ### Should I chew gum before kissing? Yes, but not during. Chewing sugar-free gum after a meal boosts saliva, which helps clear food away. Spit it out well before the kiss so there's nothing in your mouth and no strong artificial flavor. ### What should I eat before a date if I want to kiss? Anything you enjoy, as long as the last thing you eat is fresh and crisp. Ohio State researchers found that raw apple, raw lettuce and mint leaves reduced garlic breath. Go easy on garlic, onion and very sticky or sugary foods near the end of the meal. ### Why does my mouth taste bad even after I brush? The usual suspects are a coated tongue, a dry mouth, or something like garlic that reaches your breath through your bloodstream. Brush your tongue and drink water. If it persists, see a dentist, since gum disease, infections, sinus problems and acid reflux can all cause bad breath.
